title: Ballot Buddy · Alabama

boxes.title: How to read this
boxes.html: This report does not tell you who to vote for. It lays out who wrote the checks and what the public record shows. A donation is a fact about the donor; it is not proof of what the candidate will do.

footer: Sources. Who ran and who won: the Nov 3, 2026 results in the Results tab. Federal money: FEC bulk files, downloaded Nov 2, 2026. Records and positions: linked per item. State-race money: Alabama Fair Campaign Practices Act system, public files downloaded Nov 5, 2026.

cands.name: Everett Wess

money.note: Individuals gave $57,927; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $70,643. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Birmingham attorney and Democratic U.S. Senate nominee. Managing Partner of The Wess Law Firm since 2001, focused on estate planning and criminal defense. Has served as a Midfield municipal judge, a Midfield prosecutor and an Irondale public defender. State President of the Alabama New South Coalition.
cands.gaps: We could not find where Everett Wess was born or raised, or when he came to Alabama. We found no documented actions in office or stated positions on data centers, property taxes, land ownership, growth, immigration, campaign money pledges, policing, guns, abortion or school choice. His campaign site names affordable healthcare, public education, voting rights and economic opportunity as priorities but gives no specifics. His work history comes only from his campaign site, and we found no independent reporting to confirm it. We found no notable endorsements beyond informal voter-guide groups listed on Ballotpedia, and no controversies or foreign ties.

money.note: Individuals gave $2,857,770; PAC money $1,089,098; candidate's own money $50,000. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican from Enterprise, Alabama. Founded the waste-hauling company Barry Moore Industries in 1998. Served in the Alabama House (District 91) from 2010 to 2018. Has been a U.S. representative since 2021, first for AL-2 and later AL-1. Won the 2026 Republican nomination for U.S. Senate.

controversies.text: Federal records show $12,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $513 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 1 trip paid for by the American Israel Education Foundation, AIPAC's affiliate.
Missed 19 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (2.8%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 11, 2025-06-03 to 2025-06-06.

In 2014, while a state representative, Moore was charged with perjury. Prosecutors said he lied to a grand jury about telling his primary opponent to quit the race or the House Speaker would withhold money for a local project. Moore testified he told the truth. On Oct. 30, 2014, a jury found him not guilty on all four counts.

On Jan. 10, 2021, days after the Capitol attack, Moore's personal Twitter account was suspended and he then deleted it. Two of his tweets about the attack had drawn criticism. One compared arrests at the Capitol with the 2020 election, which he said was "stolen." His office said he left over "the censorship of conservative voices."

endorsements.text: For the 2026 Senate race, Ballotpedia lists endorsements from President Donald Trump, Vice President J.D. Vance, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth, Club for Growth, Gun Owners of America, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, the Alabama Farmers Federation and the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

cands.gaps: We found no documented votes, bills or statements by Moore on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign purchases of homes and land, slowing growth or conserving land and water, H-1B visas, school choice or teacher pay, or police pay and pensions. His campaign site speaks of supporting law enforcement in general terms only. Ballotpedia's page on Moore was cut off partway through his 2023-2025 House record, so we did not use anything beyond that point. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in any recent cycle. We did not find a fuller account of his move into, or years living in, any particular Alabama community beyond his Coffee County and Enterprise ties.

cands.name: Doug Jones

money.note: Covers January 2023 on, primary and general. Party-committee lines are often in-kind staff and mail.
money.source: Alabama Fair Campaign Practices Act system, downloaded Nov 5, 2026

cands.bio: Alabama attorney and Democrat. U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama 1997–2001, where he prosecuted the 1963 Birmingham church bombing case. U.S. Senator 2018–2021. Private law practice, including founding a Birmingham firm in 2013. Democratic nominee for governor in 2026.

endorsements.text: Joe Biden endorsed Jones in his 2017 U.S. Senate campaign (not the 2026 governor's race).

cands.gaps: We found no record of Jones's stated or acted-on positions on homestead property taxes, gun laws, school choice or teacher pay, policing, or limits on investor or foreign land buying. His 2026 data-center moratorium is the only land or growth stance we found. The campaign site's summary says only that he would 'support smart growth' in housing, so we did not count it as a land position. Beyond his Senate votes, we found nothing on immigration enforcement. We could read only summaries of his 2026 plans, not the full plan pages. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. Two of the pages we read were cut off before the end, so some of his Senate positions may be missing. We found no information about his work as a lawyer in private practice beyond job titles, and nothing on the size of his law firms.

cands.name: Tommy Tuberville

money.note: Covers January 2023 on, primary and general. Party-committee lines are often in-kind staff and mail.
money.source: Alabama Fair Campaign Practices Act system, downloaded Nov 5, 2026

cands.bio: Former college football head coach (Ole Miss, Auburn, Texas Tech, Cincinnati) and ESPN analyst. U.S. senator from Alabama since January 2021. Won the 2026 Republican primary with 85.5% and the general election for governor with 52.1%.

controversies.text: Missed 60 of 915 U.S. Senate votes this Congress (6.6%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-30. Longest run of misses: 8, 2026-04-27 to 2026-04-30.

Seven investors sued Tuberville and his partner John David Stroud over more than $1.7 million lost in a hedge fund. Tuberville's attorneys denied the allegations, and he settled in 2013 on undisclosed terms. Stroud pleaded guilty to securities fraud. Tuberville was not charged. Alabama's securities director said Stroud also conned Tuberville.

Tax records show the Tommy Tuberville Foundation, which Tuberville started in 2014 to help veterans, raised $289,599 over five years and spent $51,658 on charitable causes. Foundation officials said the filings don't reflect volunteer labor and donated materials used on veterans' homes. His campaign called the criticism an unfair standard.

endorsements.text: Listed in the voter guide of Conservative Christians of Alabama.

cands.gaps: We found no record of Tuberville's stance on data centers, on eliminating homestead property taxes, on limits on investor or foreign purchases of Alabama homes and land, or on growth and development policy. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. He has held no state office, so there is no state-level record. We could not establish where he lived in Alabama while coaching at Auburn from 1999 to 2008, so his length of Alabama residence is not scored. His campaign site describes his school-choice and public-safety plans only in general terms.

cands.name: John Wahl

money.note: Covers January 2023 on, primary and general. Party-committee lines are often in-kind staff and mail.
money.source: Alabama Fair Campaign Practices Act system, downloaded Nov 5, 2026

cands.bio: Butterfly farmer and businessman from Limestone County, Alabama. Chaired the Alabama Republican Party from 2021 to 2026 and served as a Republican National Committee vice chair. Chairs the Alabama Public Library Service board. Won the 2026 election for lieutenant governor.

controversies.text: In 2020 Wahl showed a Limestone County poll worker a 'regional press secretary' badge from the State Auditor's office as ID. Then-Secretary of State John Merrill and Wes Allen forwarded complaints to the attorney general. Wahl said he'd left his wallet at home. Ex-Auditor Jim Zeigler said he approved the badge and it was professionally printed.

In 2026 a former legislator challenged Wahl's eligibility for lieutenant governor, citing a Tennessee driver's license and 2020 Tennessee voter registration. The state Republican Party's steering committee dismissed it without a hearing, reportedly on a 9-9 tie broken by the acting chair. Wahl called it a 'political hit job'. His lawyer said a second residence doesn't cancel Alabama residency.

In 2025, Limestone County Republican committee members accused Wahl and his brother of a conflict of interest through their consulting firm, WT&S, which was paid by candidates and the party. The recording and records were reportedly sent to state officials and law enforcement. Wahl has said party bylaws required him to separate from the firm. No finding has been reported.

endorsements.text: President Donald Trump endorsed Wahl; the campaign quotes him: 'Complete and Total Endorsement. RUN, JOHN, RUN!'
Conservative Christians of Alabama listed Wahl among its voter guide recommendations.

cands.gaps: We found no statements or actions by Wahl on data centers or on slowing growth and protecting land. We found nothing on limiting out-of-state, investor or foreign buyers of homes and land, and nothing on teacher pay. We found no pledge on refusing foreign-linked or big-donor money. He has held no elected office, so there is no legislative or executive record to review. The sources do not say how many people he employs or how large his farm's budget is. His party-chair fundraising totals differ between sources ($2.8 million by 2023 in one, $7.5 million in another), and the party audit had not been released. We found no documented foreign government ties. His residency and voter-registration questions are described only in secondary reporting, and no formal investigation or court finding is reported.

cands.bio: Alabama attorney and Republican nominee for Attorney General. Former legislative counsel to U.S. Sen. Jeff Sessions and Vice President at the Alabama Policy Institute. Chief counsel to Attorney General Steve Marshall since March 2017. Won the 2026 general election.

controversies.text: In 2025 First Principles Action, a nonprofit with a Nashville address, gave Robertson's attorney general campaign $1 million, then $100,000 more. Opponent Jay Mitchell called it dark money. Alabama Daily News reported that Alabama law allows accepting the money. No violation has been reported.

In July 2023 a Corrections Department lawyer told a legislative committee the attorney general's office had blocked settling federal prison lawsuits. Robertson, then chief counsel, wrote that this was false and the state was willing to resume settlement talks. Corrections said its lawyer meant the office's stance against a consent decree. No finding was reported.

cands.gaps: We could not confirm her Alabama State Bar admission or standing from the pages available. Her birth city and the town where she attended school were not given beyond Dallas County. We found no statements or actions from her on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buying, growth and land protection, school choice or teacher pay, or gun policy. We found no specific cases, opinions or filings she personally handled as chief counsel, only general descriptions. Her campaign site lists endorsement headlines (including from the NRA Political Victory Fund and county sheriffs), but only as headlines, so we could not read or verify them, and Ballotpedia lists no endorsements. She did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey. The Wikipedia claims about her positions and the two controversies come from a single page that we could not cross-check with news reports.

platform.summary: This is the platform Ballot Buddy scores against, adapted to Alabama. James Fishback ran on it in the 2026 Republican primary for Florida governor: an affordability and land-protection message on top of a conservative base. Details that only applied to Florida have been swapped for Alabama. It's one yardstick, chosen by this guide, and not a neutral one.

planks.title: Ban data centers statewide
planks.promise: Ban AI and hyperscale data centers in every Alabama county through statewide preemption of county approvals, to protect farmland, water and electric bills.
planks.tells_for: Votes or stated positions to ban, put a moratorium on, or preempt data-center approvals; opposing data-center rezonings on farmland; refusing data-center-industry money.
planks.tells_against: Votes to approve or fast-track a data center, rezone farmland for one, or give it tax breaks; campaigning on attracting data centers or AI infrastructure.

planks.title: Eliminate homestead property taxes
planks.promise: Eliminate property taxes on Alabama residents' primary homes (not second homes, short-term rentals or mega-estates), paid for by rolling local government spending back.
planks.tells_for: Votes for homestead exemption increases, assessment caps or abolition; pledges to cut or end homestead taxes; pledges to cut local spending or tax rates.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements for raising property taxes; opposing homestead tax relief; defending local government revenue growth.

planks.title: Alabama homes and land for Alabamians
planks.promise: Ban private equity and Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, tax out-of-state vacation-home buyers, and keep foreign adversaries from owning Alabama land.
planks.tells_for: Supporting limits on institutional or foreign buyers of homes and land; proposing taxes or caps on out-of-state or investor purchases.
planks.tells_against: Opposing limits on corporate or foreign land buying; courting institutional or foreign real-estate capital.

planks.title: Slow growth, protect land and water
planks.promise: Develop slower and smarter, stop overdevelopment, and conserve Alabama's state parks, waterways and natural lands.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements to hold or tighten growth limits, require approvals for large developments, deny rezonings of farmland or open space, fund conservation; refusing developer money.
planks.tells_against: Votes to expand development boundaries, waive development oversight, preempt local growth limits, approve large developer land deals over resident objections; heavy developer funding.

planks.title: Alabama workers first: end H-1B
planks.promise: End H-1B abuse with fines that wipe out any savings from replacing a Alabama worker, keep H-1B workers off state contracts, raise foreign-student tuition, and back strong immigration enforcement and deportations.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, E-Verify, detention of criminal illegal immigrants, limiting H-1B or guest-worker displacement of Americans.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against immigration-enforcement bills; defending H-1B or guest-worker expansion or sanctuary-style policies.

planks.title: No foreign or big-donor money
planks.promise: Refuse contributions from foreign-affiliated groups (naming AIPAC) and run against donor capture.
planks.tells_for: Stated pledges to refuse foreign-linked, corporate-PAC, developer or out-of-state big-donor money; small-dollar funded campaigns.
planks.tells_against: Documented reliance on developer, foreign-linked or mega-donor or PAC money; stated openness to it.

planks.title: Back police, restore order
planks.promise: Raise pay and improve pensions for law enforcement and corrections officers, charge teen takeovers as felonies, surge state resources on homelessness, and remove prosecutors who refuse to prosecute.
planks.tells_for: Votes or positions raising penalties for rioting or disorder, funding or improving pay and pensions for officers, supporting police, tough-on-crime prosecution.
planks.tells_against: Votes cutting officer pensions or benefits; opposing penalties for public disorder; defund-style positions.

planks.title: Defend the Second Amendment
planks.promise: Eliminate Red Flag laws, end restrictions on suppressors, bump stocks and forced-reset triggers, and oppose raising gun purchase ages; also pull Flock cameras and stop Palantir contracts.
planks.tells_for: Votes for permitless carry and stand-your-ground, against red-flag laws and new purchase-age limits; pledges to oppose new gun restrictions.
planks.tells_against: Votes for red-flag laws, purchase-age or waiting-period laws, assault-weapon or magazine limits.

planks.title: Pro-life, no exceptions
planks.promise: Life begins at conception; shut down Alabama's abortion clinics and replace them with crisis pregnancy centers, plus paid maternity leave.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for abortion bans, waiting periods or other abortion restrictions; support for pregnancy centers.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against abortion restrictions; support for abortion-access measures.

planks.title: School choice and teacher pay
planks.promise: Universal school choice funded toward parity with public schools, a state homeschool commissioner, and a 25% raise for teachers.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for vouchers, charters or universal choice and for raising teacher pay.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against voucher or charter expansion or school-choice funding.
